paras: The threatened lynching of John B. Hunter took place in Culbertson, Nebraska, in June 1888, when a crowd gathered to lynch Hunter, a hardware merchant held for the shooting death of farmer Harry B. Hull. According to the Omaha Bee, about 200 people besieged the sheriff's residence where he was held, but no attack followed, and Hunter was taken to Lincoln for safe keeping. He was tried at Culbertson in December and given a twelve-month sentence, which one dispatch called light.

Hull and the Hunters had quarreled for some days over a line fence and over a mule of the Hunters' that Hull had taken up for damages to his farm. On June 5, in a Culbertson billiard hall, Hunter's father, G. V. Hunter, quarreled with Hull, who struck him with a cue. John B. Hunter then fired twice, and Hull died about fifteen minutes later at the Grand Central hotel.

The Omaha Herald's correspondent wrote that the Hunters had set out to provoke Hull and that the killing was premeditated, while the Bee's correspondent called the Hunters 'quarrelsome and dangerous characters.' A coroner's jury found that Hull died by a pistol in Hunter's hands, and Hunter was promptly arrested.

Talk of lynching began on the day of the shooting, when the Bee's correspondent reported 'some talk of lynch law being resorted to to-night' and the Herald's noted street talk of a mob. In a dispatch dated June 7, the day Hull was buried, the Bee reported that Hunter, held at the sheriff's residence, was besieged by a crowd of 200 'anxious to lynch him.' The McCook Tribune, published in a nearby town, wrote that a 'neck-tie party' had been strongly threatened but fell through for lack of a leader. By the Tribune's account, Hunter was taken to Lincoln on Wednesday night, June 6, for safe keeping.

No arrests of anyone in the crowd are reported. Hunter's trial opened in district court at Culbertson in early December, with Judge Mason of Lincoln for the defense and Judge House and J. Byron Jennings for the prosecution. A McCook dispatch of December 14 reported that the trial had closed and that Hunter would go to Lincoln for twelve months.

Coverage came entirely from the white press, led by the Omaha Bee, whose Culbertson correspondent sent the first report and the two-sentence item headed 'Want to Lynch Him.' Neither the Bee nor the McCook Tribune condemned the crowd; the Tribune used the light phrase 'neck-tie party.' Brief news columns in the Hope Pioneer, the Iowa County Democrat and the Frontier of O'Neill, Nebraska, carried the shooting as a feud killing, and only the Frontier repeated the talk of lynching.

Later reports took Hull's side: the Bee predicted that the Hunters would spend money 'to defeat justice,' and the Press and Daily Dakotaian headed the sentence 'A Murderer's Light Sentence,' calling it the third Culbertson murder in five years in which the killer went free or received the lightest possible sentence.

The accounts differ on timing, since the Bee dates the siege to the dispatch of June 7, while the Tribune places Hunter's removal to Lincoln on the night of June 6. They also differ on the shooting itself, which the Culbertson correspondents placed in the morning and the Tribune in the evening, and on the wound, given as behind the ear in the Herald account and through the heart in the Dakotaian.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of John B. Hunter
bases: A crowd reported at 200 gathered at the sheriff's residence intending to lynch a prisoner accused of murder, but no attack or killing is reported (A2, A4).
Hunter was not killed: he was removed to Lincoln and later tried and sentenced (A4, A9); the crowd of 200 that wanted to lynch him for the killing of Hull makes this a threatened lynching only (A2).

The Omaha Bee's Culbertson correspondent and the McCook Tribune independently report lynching threats against Hunter after the shooting, though only the Bee describes a crowd besieging the sheriff's residence (A1, A2, A4, A7).

accounts.label: Omaha Bee Culbertson correspondent
accounts.gist: Hunter 'deliberately' shot Hull before noon on June 5 over his father's dispute with Hull; there was talk of lynching that night, and on June 7 a crowd of 200 besieged the sheriff's residence wanting to lynch him.

accounts.label: McCook Tribune (neighboring town)
accounts.gist: The shooting took place Tuesday evening after Hull struck the elder Hunter with a cue in a dispute over a trespassing mule; a lynching was strongly threatened but fell through for lack of a leader, and Hunter was taken to Lincoln on Wednesday night.

accounts.label: Omaha Herald correspondent (reprinted)
accounts.gist: The Hunters planned to provoke Hull, who struck the father with a cue, and John Hunter shot him through the head; Hunter was promptly arrested and there was street talk of a mob.

framing.detail: The Omaha Bee reported the crowd of 200 'anxious to lynch him' in a two-sentence item headed 'Want to Lynch Him,' without comment, after calling the Hunters 'quarrelsome and dangerous characters.'
The McCook Tribune used the jocular 'neck-tie party' and said the plan fell through 'for lack of a leader,' without condemning it.
Brief state and national news columns carried the shooting as a feud killing; only the Frontier repeated the talk of lynching.
Later dispatches sided against Hunter, predicting money would be spent 'to defeat justice' and calling the twelve-month term 'A Murderer's Light Sentence.'

info: Hull was shot on Tuesday, June 5, 1888; lynching talk was reported that night, and a crowd besieged the sheriff's residence according to a dispatch dated June 7, the day of Hull's burial
Culbertson, Nebraska; the shooting took place in a billiard hall (named in one account as Trout & Manarron's on Taylor avenue), and the crowd gathered at the sheriff's residence
John B. Hunter, a Culbertson hardware merchant, was the target of the lynching threats; no race is given in any report
Accused of shooting and killing Harry B. Hull, a farmer living near Culbertson, after a quarrel between Hull and Hunter's father, G. V. Hunter
A crowd of Culbertson-area residents; no names given
Hunter was sentenced to twelve months, to be served at Lincoln
